content.headline: Ukraine says Starlink speed limits disrupted missions as Musk points to US role
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine says Starlink limits disrupted missions
content.standfirst: Ukraine says a speed restriction on Starlink-connected drones disrupted military missions, while Elon Musk says the US government controls its military-grade Starshield service. The source and purpose of the restrictions remain unclear.

image.caption: Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy meets UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London.

sources.originalTitle: Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds
Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access
Zelenskyj føler sig forrådt af Trump - en appel til Europa, mener ekspert
In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll

segments.body: Ukraine says drones travelling above 160km/h lost Starlink connectivity, disrupting some battlefield missions. Connectivity was partly restored by Wednesday evening, according to former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov. Musk said limits on Starshield, a separate military-grade service, are set by the US military and ultimately the president; he described Starlink as a civilian service for defensive use.

segments.title: Military and diplomatic consequences
segments.body: Experts cited by the BBC say Starlink supports communications across Ukraine’s forces and helps drones and command posts share information. Ukraine says it was not warned about the restrictions. The US government has not commented, and the gather does not establish who ordered the speed limits or why.

The Guardian’s analysis argues that the restrictions could put Ukrainian civilians at greater risk by weakening air defences against faster Russian drones, while having less effect on Ukraine’s deep strikes inside Russia. A Ukrainian soldier cited by the paper said mid-range operations could fall sharply, but commanders were seeking alternatives.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis distinguishes between drone missions: it says the restrictions may have a limited effect on deep strikes, but could seriously weaken air defences protecting civilians.

content.headline: Two container ships sink near the Strait of Hormuz as attacks on shipping rise
content.shortHeadline: Two ships sink amid rising attacks near Hormuz
content.standfirst: Two container ships have sunk after incidents near the strategic waterway, as maritime authorities report a rise in attacks. Iran says one vessel hit a mine; UK authorities say both were struck by unidentified projectiles.

sources.originalTitle: Two container ships sink near strait of Hormuz amid surge in Iranian attacks

segments.body: The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride sank on Wednesday after an attack the previous day. The Antigua- and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank hours later; it had been hit by a projectile on 23 September, according to International Maritime Organization data. UK Maritime Trade Operations reported at least five incidents involving commercial vessels around Hormuz in the previous 48 hours.

segments.title: Conflicting accounts and possible motives
segments.body: Iran said the GFS Pride hit a naval mine while travelling on an unauthorised route. UK Maritime Trade Operations said both ships had been hit by unidentified projectiles. The report describes a marked increase in attacks, but responsibility and the motive remain unclear; claims that Iran is seeking to close the waterway or affect US fuel prices are attributed analysis, not confirmed facts.

content.headline: Students attack government buildings as protests spread in Albania
content.shortHeadline: Violent student protests spread in Albania
content.standfirst: Thousands of students in Tirana are protesting over university conditions and job prospects. Buildings were attacked and part of the education ministry was set on fire, as police used tear gas and water cannon.

image.caption: Protesters gather in Tirana, Albania’s capital.

sources.originalTitle: Student protesters attack government buildings in Albania

segments.body: Thousands of students took to the streets of Tirana for a second day of anti-government protests. Demonstrators attacked several government buildings and businesses; part of the education ministry was set on fire. Riot police used tear gas and water cannon to disperse the crowds.

segments.title: Wider anger
segments.body: The protests began with calls for better university conditions and job prospects, but one demonstrator told Reuters they were also about anger at the political system. The demonstrations follow months of protests calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign, sparked by a tourism project linked to Jared Kushner and allegations of corruption and a lack of transparency.

content.headline: US data centre backlash becomes an issue in midterm election campaigns
content.shortHeadline: Data centre backlash reaches US midterm campaigns
content.standfirst: Opposition to large data centre projects is prompting politicians in both parties to reconsider their positions, with residents raising concerns about their effects on local resources, neighbourhoods and public services.

image.caption: The BBC’s Shaimaa Khalil speaks with residents in Arizona about data centre expansion.

sources.originalTitle: How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections

segments.body: Residents in several US states are organising against data centre projects, citing their scale, noise and demands on water, energy and local infrastructure. The BBC reports that community groups opposing the developments more than doubled to 833 in the first months of this year, according to Data Center Watch.

segments.title: Political pressure and open questions
segments.body: The issue is reaching election campaigns, with candidates from both parties responding to local opposition. Some politicians have proposed temporary pauses or limits, while President Donald Trump has criticised the backlash. Research cited by the BBC found a new data centre creates 100 to 200 local jobs—fewer than industry advocates claim—and has little effect on local wages.

Many of the pauses and proposals are temporary, and it remains uncertain whether politicians will maintain them as public attention shifts. Developers say some projects are designed to manage their energy and water use, but the BBC reports that community opposition can be strong even where developers offer such assurances.

content.headline: Nepal proposes climate cooperation between India and China in the Himalayas
content.shortHeadline: Nepal urges India and China to cooperate on Himalayan risks
content.standfirst: Nepal wants its two powerful neighbours to share climate data and coordinate disaster response in the Himalayas. Neither country has formally responded, and earlier attempts at joint work have made little progress.

image.caption: Flooding in Nepal has highlighted the need for cooperation on Himalayan disaster risks.

sources.originalTitle: India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats

segments.body: Nepal’s prime minister has proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to improve cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise. The idea is at an early stage, and neither India nor China has formally responded.

segments.title: A shared risk, difficult cooperation
segments.body: Rising temperatures are accelerating glacier retreat and increasing risks including landslides and glacial lake floods, which can cross borders and threaten communities downstream. But past cooperation has been limited: an India-China glacier research initiative agreed in 2009 went nowhere, and data-sharing agreements on rivers originating in Tibet have expired or been interrupted.

Experts cited by the BBC say countries could start with practical steps such as identifying high-risk lakes, agreeing monitoring standards and sharing urgent warnings. They also warn that data on river flows or terrain can carry military significance in a region where India and China have unresolved border disputes.

content.headline: North Korea says it test-fired cruise missiles from a submarine
content.shortHeadline: North Korea reports submarine-launched cruise missile test
content.standfirst: North Korea says it test-fired two cruise missiles over the Sea of Japan, describing the exercise as a test of its naval capability. The report comes amid rising tensions with South Korea.

sources.originalTitle: Nordkorea tester missiler fra ubåd

segments.body: North Korea’s state news agency KCNA says the country test-fired two cruise missiles from a submarine over the Sea of Japan. The report said the test was intended to confirm the navy’s operational capability and the reliability of its deterrence; those claims come from North Korea.

The test follows rising tensions with South Korea after an explosion in the Demilitarized Zone in September injured three South Korean soldiers. Both countries have since tested more advanced missile systems, according to the report.

content.headline: Reform UK candidates filmed making racist and violent comments, investigation'
content.shortHeadline: Reform UK faces new crisis over candidates’ filmed comments
content.standfirst: An ITV undercover investigation has prompted three councillors to leave Reform UK and Nigel Farage to postpone an announcement. The party says it is investigating, while further footage is expected.

image.caption: Reform UK councillor Alan Feeney was filmed making racist comments.

sources.originalTitle: Reform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and extreme comments

segments.body: ITV footage showed Reform UK councillors and candidates making racist, misogynistic and violent comments. Among them, Solihull deputy mayor Alan Feeney was filmed describing Asian homeowners as “parasites”. Feeney and two other councillors have left the party; one of the three says he resigned for personal reasons.

segments.title: Party response and further scrutiny
segments.body: Reform says it is investigating and has suspended some members, while accusing ITV and its production company of using deceptive methods to gain access to its headquarters. Farage postponed a planned announcement as the party prepared for further revelations, including footage involving staff at its London office.

The investigation comes after Farage pledged to remove extremists and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out checks on candidates. The reporting also notes other scrutiny facing Reform, including an earlier undercover investigation and a parliamentary standards inquiry concerning a £5m gift to Farage.

content.headline: Sally Rooney and publisher withdraw her books from UK supply over Palestine Act
content.shortHeadline: Sally Rooney books will no longer be supplied in the UK
content.standfirst: The Irish novelist says UK law could make supplying her books a criminal offence because she intends to give royalties to Palestine Action, which is proscribed in the UK. Existing physical stock can remain on booksellers’ shelves.

image.caption: Sally Rooney’s novels will no longer be supplied to UK booksellers.

sources.originalTitle: Sally Rooney books withdrawn in UK over Palestine Action support
Sally Rooney stopper salg af romaner i Storbritannien efter støtte til Palestine Action

segments.body: Sally Rooney and her publisher, Faber, have agreed that her books will no longer be supplied to UK booksellers. Rooney says fulfilling publication contracts could constitute a “serious criminal offence” because she intends to use royalties to support Palestine Action, which the UK proscribed as a terrorist organisation in 2025.

segments.title: Existing copies and legal challenge
segments.body: Ebook editions have been removed from sale, but booksellers can continue selling physical copies already in stock, Waterstones told the BBC. The proscription is being challenged in court, with a legal hearing due at the Supreme Court next month; thousands of people have been arrested or charged over alleged support for the group, but none have yet gone to trial.

Faber says it cannot pass UK earnings on to Rooney and calls that an unacceptable situation. Rooney says she accepts the consequences of her position. Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori described the withdrawal as an attack on free speech; that is her response to the decision, not a court finding about the law’s application.

content.headline: UK pledges £17m for repairs to Chornobyl shelter damaged by Russian strike
content.shortHeadline: UK pledges £17m for Chornobyl repairs
content.standfirst: The funding is intended to repair the protective shelter and ventilation at the decommissioned nuclear plant, damaged in a Russian drone strike last year. The announcement follows Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s visit to London.

sources.originalTitle: Ukraine war briefing: UK pledges £17m to repair Chornobyl attack damage amid fears of slipping US support
Storbritannien klar til at give penge til reparationer af Tjernobyl
Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access

segments.body: The UK will provide £17m towards repairs to the protective shelter and ventilation at the Chornobyl nuclear power plant in Ukraine. The structure was damaged in a Russian drone strike last year, and the UK says the repairs are needed to address longer-term safety and environmental risks.

The funding was announced after Prime Minister Andy Burnham hosted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Downing Street. The UK said it would also accelerate delivery of lightweight missiles to Ukraine as it seeks to strengthen support amid uncertainty over the US commitment.

content.headline: Russell Brand trial hears prosecution allegations from six women
content.shortHeadline: Brand denies charges as trial hears six women’s allegations
content.standfirst: Prosecutors allege that Russell Brand raped or sexually assaulted six women between 1999 and 2009. He denies all charges; jurors have begun hearing evidence in a trial expected to last six weeks.

image.caption: Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
Russell Brand was ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator, court told
Russell Brand was ‘ruthless sexual predator’ – five key takeaways from trial so far

segments.body: Russell Brand denies three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. The prosecution says six women who did not know one another came forward independently with allegations spanning 1999 to 2009. These are allegations being tested in court, not findings of guilt.

segments.title: Evidence begins
segments.body: The jury has heard accounts of the alleged incidents and testimony from Brand’s former flatmate, Mark Pinheiro. Pinheiro told jurors that Brand said he may have gone “a bit too far” with a woman at the 1999 Labour Party conference. The defence questioned whether he remembered the comment accurately; he said he was sure of it.

Brand has told police he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity and said accounts may have been reinvented or imagined after media reporting, according to the prosecution’s opening. The trial is expected to last six weeks.

content.headline: UK sanctions regime expands to cover enablers of illegal settlement activity
content.shortHeadline: New UK sanctions powers extend to settlement enablers
content.standfirst: The new regime allows ministers to target people and organisations suspected of enabling serious breaches of international law, including unlawful settlement activity. It takes effect on Thursday but requires parliamentary approval.

image.caption: Election billboards in the West Bank, where bids for a new settlement have been invited.

sources.originalTitle: New UK sanctions powers will enable action against supporters of illegal Israeli settlements

segments.body: The UK’s expanded global human rights sanctions regime adds grounds covering serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian aid and serious violations of the right to liberty and security. It also allows action against those suspected of facilitating, financing or benefiting from qualifying conduct.

segments.title: How the powers may apply
segments.body: The Guardian reports that unlawful settlement activity can fall within the new rules, which can impose asset freezes, travel bans and restrictions on making funds available. The new urgent procedure allows the UK to mirror sanctions imposed by several partner countries for up to 112 days while preparing a separate UK case.

The regime comes into force on Thursday and must be endorsed by MPs and peers within 28 days. The UK government is also working with European partners on separate proposals concerning British trade with unlawful Israeli settlements.

content.headline: UK hospitality firms to offer up to 100,000 placements for young people
content.shortHeadline: Hospitality scheme offers young people up to 100,000 placements
content.standfirst: Restaurants, pubs and hotels will offer short placements to 18- to 24-year-olds not in work, education or training under a government-backed scheme. A review of youth unemployment is expected soon.

image.caption: The scheme aims to give young people a first step into work.

sources.originalTitle: UK hospitality sector to offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people out of work

segments.body: Hospitality businesses including Nando’s, Burger King, Premier Inn and Fuller’s plan to offer up to 100,000 placements over three years for 18- to 24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training. Placements can last up to four weeks and are intended to provide a route into work.

The initiative is being developed with the Department for Work and Pensions and follows a similar scheme for retailers. The government says the placements will help young people gain skills and confidence; the report notes that a review of youth unemployment by Alan Milburn is expected soon after the autumn Budget.

content.headline: Greenland says US oil and mineral exploration must follow Greenlandic law
content.shortHeadline: Greenland says US resource projects must follow its laws
content.standfirst: After Donald Trump claimed extensive exploration was being prepared in Greenland, Denmark’s Foreign Ministry said US investors have no special access to the territory’s resources. Greenland’s government has taken responsibility for the sector.

image.caption: Greenland, Denmark and the United States signed a security and defence agreement in September.

sources.originalTitle: Ministerium: Amerikanske olieprojekter skal ske efter grønlandsk lov
Trump puster til ambitioner om amerikansk olie-eventyr i Grønland

segments.body: Donald Trump said extensive exploration for oil, gas and minerals was being prepared in Greenland. Denmark’s Foreign Ministry responded that any US exploration must follow relevant Greenlandic law and that American investors have no preferential access to resources over investors from other NATO, EU or partner countries.

segments.title: What is known about current activity
segments.body: A senior Greenlandic official told CNN there are smaller exploration projects underway, but said it could take years for them to become operational and that activity is far from a massive oil exploration campaign. The Foreign Ministry did not confirm Trump’s claim about a coming large-scale effort.

The ministry said the September security and defence agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the US does not change Greenland’s authority over resources. Neither the Danish nor Greenlandic government had commented directly on Trump’s post at the time of the report.

content.headline: Wolt delivery made it easier for a woman to order vodka, DR reports
content.shortHeadline: Wolt says user-exclusion option was missed in alcohol case
content.standfirst: A woman in treatment for alcohol misuse says rapid delivery made it easier to order vodka. Wolt says staff failed to use an existing option that can block a customer from buying alcohol and says it will inform support teams.

image.caption: A woman says easy access to alcohol delivery made it harder to resist ordering vodka.

sources.originalTitle: Da hun for et år siden opdagede, at man kunne få to flasker vodka lige så nemt som en durumrulle, eskalerede hendes alkoholforbrug

segments.body: A woman identified by DR as Anna says that being able to order vodka through Wolt contributed to an increase in her drinking. She says she asked the company to block her from buying alcohol through the app, but support staff told her this was not possible and suggested deleting her account.

segments.title: Company response and proposed safeguards
segments.body: Wolt later told DR that customers can be excluded from buying alcohol through customer support, and described the handling of Anna’s request as human error. The company said it would ensure support staff know about the option. Alcohol & Society says easy access can worsen alcohol problems and plans to recommend that lawmakers consider limits on delivery sales.

content.headline: Plastic pellets wash up on Denmark’s west coast, threatening birds
content.shortHeadline: Plastic pellets spread along Denmark’s west coast
content.standfirst: Tiny pellets have been found on beaches from Rømø to Løkken and are believed to match material lost in a shipping accident near Newcastle. Their size makes cleanup difficult, and conservationists warn birds may eat them.

image.caption: Small plastic pellets have washed up on west coast beaches and are difficult to remove.

sources.originalTitle: Hele vestkysten er ramt af plastikkugler, og det er 'en stort set umulig opgave'

segments.body: Small plastic pellets have been found along the coast from the German island of Sylt to Løkken. They are believed to match pellets released in a shipping accident near Newcastle this summer, when the Port of Tyne says almost 18 tonnes entered the sea.

segments.title: Cleanup and wildlife risks
segments.body: The pellets are smaller than five millimetres and can be difficult to collect with ordinary beach-cleaning equipment. A local bird conservation representative warned that birds may mistake them for food; if swallowed, the pellets can accumulate in their stomachs.

content.headline: DNA match leads to arrest in Aarhus forest assault case
content.shortHeadline: DNA match leads to arrest in Aarhus assault case
content.standfirst: Police arrested a 19-year-old in connection with an assault in Riis Skov on 27 September. They are also investigating whether he is linked to a similar July incident, but say the second case remains under investigation.

sources.originalTitle: Mand anholdt i sag om overfald i skov

segments.body: East Jutland Police say a DNA match led them to arrest a 19-year-old in connection with an assault in Riis Skov on 27 September. Police planned to seek his remand in custody. He is a suspect; the report does not establish guilt.

Police have also examined a 12 July assault because the incidents happened relatively close to one another and had similar circumstances. They say they are confident about the September case but are continuing to investigate whether the two are linked.

content.headline: Man charged after fatal stabbing in central Odense
content.shortHeadline: 81-year-old charged after fatal Odense stabbing
content.standfirst: Police say a 65-year-old man has died after a stabbing in central Odense. An 81-year-old local man has been arrested and charged with murder; it is not known whether he admits the charge.

image.caption: Police at the scene of the stabbing in central Odense.

sources.originalTitle: 81-årig anholdt i sagen om knivdrab

segments.body: A 65-year-old man from Odense municipality died after being stabbed in Nedergade on Wednesday morning, police said. An 81-year-old man from the municipality has been arrested and charged with murder. He is due in court on Thursday.
Police said earlier that there was no indication the incident was gang-related and that there was no danger to the wider public. The report says it is not known whether the suspect admits the charge.

content.headline: Parties split over proposed interview for Danish citizenship applicant
content.shortHeadline: Parties divided over citizenship applicant interview
content.standfirst: Several parties want a citizenship applicant questioned over Facebook posts that Liberal Alliance says praise Hamas. She denies supporting Hamas and says she is willing to attend; other parties oppose or question the proposal.

image.caption: A member of parliament at the opening of the Danish Parliament.

sources.originalTitle: Facebookopslag kan få politiske konsekvenser: Flere partier vil indkalde kvinde til samtale

segments.body: Liberal Alliance says Facebook posts from 2024 by a woman seeking Danish citizenship praise Hamas and former Hamas leaders, and wants her interviewed by Parliament’s citizenship committee. The woman denies supporting Hamas and told Politiken she would be willing to explain the posts.

segments.title: Political disagreement
segments.body: The Danish People’s Party, Denmark Democrats and Conservatives support an interview. The Social Democrats say applicants on the bill will be checked again and question whether a separate interview is needed now. The Red-Green Alliance opposes questioning someone over political views, while the woman’s claims remain disputed.

The government plans to reintroduce a citizenship bill covering about 2,000 applicants, while a working group examines possible screening for anti-democratic views. It takes a committee majority to summon an applicant for an interview.

content.headline: Parents report extra costs and pressure around Denmark’s public schools
content.shortHeadline: Parents describe hidden costs around public schooling
content.standfirst: Parents say class funds, events and other school-related expenses add up, with one mother calculating more than 300 kroner a month for two children. They say the pressure can also involve time and the risk of children feeling excluded.

image.caption: Parents say school-related activities can bring extra costs for families.

sources.originalTitle: Mor lagde skjulte småbeløb i folkeskolen sammen – resultatet overraskede hende

segments.body: Parents told TV 2 that costs linked to public school can include class funds, costumes, school events and trips. One parent’s review of spending for two children found the total averaged more than 300 kroner a month over the previous school year; another parent offered an illustrative estimate of 1,400 kroner for one child over a school year.

segments.title: Costs and participation
segments.body: Parents said the concern was not only the amount of individual expenses but whether children could feel left out when families could not pay. Some also described pressure to attend events that can conflict with work and family commitments. The report notes that costs and expectations vary between schools and classes.

content.headline: Farmers seek answers after incorrect nitrogen calculations
content.shortHeadline: Incorrect nitrogen calculations leave farmers reworking plans
content.standfirst: Farmers in northern Jutland say incorrect figures for next year’s nitrogen limits have forced them to revisit field plans. Aarhus University has apologised and says correcting the calculations will take about a week.

image.caption: Farmers seek advice after errors in nitrogen-limit calculations.

sources.originalTitle: Telefonen gløder: Landmænd søger svar efter fejlagtige beregninger

segments.body: Farmers have received incorrect information about how much nitrogen they may emit from next year, according to Aarhus University, which produced the calculations. The university has apologised and says it expects corrections to take about a week.

A representative of the Agillix farmers’ association says farmers are frustrated because some had already used the figures to plan work in their fields. The association is helping members and plans meetings to discuss the issue.

content.headline: PSG overwhelm Manchester City before a fierce second-half fightback
content.shortHeadline: PSG overwhelm City before second-half fightback
content.standfirst: Paris St-Germain led 3-0 at half-time at the Etihad, then held off a Manchester City rally to win 4-2. The result came on Pep Guardiola’s return to the stadium amid uncertainty over City’s financial case.

image.caption: Manchester City and PSG meet at the Etihad in the Champions League.

sources.originalTitle: Guardiola's return, Man City's defiance - and a game of glorious chaos
PSG on 'different level' - are they building greatest European dynasty?

segments.body: PSG tore through City in the first half, with Désiré Doué, Ousmane Dembélé and Vitinha scoring to put the visitors 3-0 ahead. City responded after the break, creating chances and scoring twice, but PSG added a fourth to secure a 4-2 Champions League win.

segments.title: A bid for a third European crown
segments.body: PSG are pursuing a third successive Champions League title. BBC Sport’s account of the club’s rise says the shift towards a more coherent team of younger players under Luis Enrique followed years of lavish spending; the 4-2 win offered another display of their attacking strength.

perspectives.body: BBC Sport’s historical comparison puts PSG’s prospective run alongside Europe’s past dominant sides, while noting that a team’s legacy can extend beyond its trophy count.

content.headline: Aston Villa hit Fenerbahce for six in their biggest European win
content.shortHeadline: Villa hit Fenerbahce for six in record European win
content.standfirst: Nicolas Jackson scored twice as Aston Villa recorded a 6-0 Champions League victory, their biggest win in Europe. It was also their first home win of the season and a boost after a difficult start at Villa Park.

image.caption: Aston Villa’s 6-0 win over Fenerbahce was their biggest European victory.

sources.originalTitle: Jackson steps up again as Aston Villa revival continues

segments.body: Villa were three goals ahead by half-time against Fenerbahce and finished with a 6-0 win. Jackson’s double helped set up the result; Ross Barkley also scored twice, with Johan Manzambi and Tammy Abraham completing the tally. It was Villa’s first home win this season and a club record in Europe.

segments.title: Progress, with more work to do
segments.body: Unai Emery said the result was an important step but that his side still needed time to improve, after a summer that brought 10 new players. Jackson has scored four times in his last three games, helping Villa adjust to the departure of Ollie Watkins.

content.headline: Barcola’s first hat-trick leads Liverpool to a 6-3 win over LASK
content.shortHeadline: Barcola hits first hat-trick as Liverpool beat LASK 6-3
content.standfirst: Bradley Barcola answered questions about his form with three goals in Linz, while Florian Wirtz also impressed. Liverpool returned to winning ways, though the match’s uneven second half offered some reason for caution.

image.caption: Bradley Barcola celebrates his hat-trick against LASK.

sources.originalTitle: On night of mayhem for Liverpool, Barcola arrives in style

segments.body: Barcola scored his first career hat-trick as Liverpool beat LASK 6-3 in the Champions League. His two first-half finishes and a second-half tap-in helped turn a dominant opening period into a comfortable lead; Wirtz also contributed an assist.

segments.title: A caveat to the big win
segments.body: Liverpool had 19 shots by half-time, but conceded three times after the break. BBC Sport pundit Stephen Warnock cautioned against reading too much into the performance, noting LASK had been winless in their previous four matches and saying a sterner test would follow.

content.headline: Sonay Kartal upsets Bencic as Sabalenka suffers another early Wuhan exit
content.shortHeadline: Kartal beats Bencic as Sabalenka exits Wuhan
content.standfirst: Kartal, ranked 170th after a six-month injury absence, beat world number 12 Belinda Bencic in straight sets. Aryna Sabalenka then lost despite saving nine match points, making it two consecutive early exits for the world number two.

image.caption: Sonay Kartal has returned to the WTA Tour after a six-month injury absence.

sources.originalTitle: Briton Kartal causes upset before Sabalenka loses again

segments.body: Britain’s Sonay Kartal beat ninth seed Bencic 6-0 7-5 to reach the Wuhan Open third round. The win was the second biggest of Kartal’s career by ranking. She said she trusted she could regain her level, but still had to find a way to sustain it.

segments.title: Sabalenka beaten after saving nine match points
segments.body: Sabalenka lost 3-6 6-4 7-6 (7-5) to Ann Li after saving nine match points. It was her second successive defeat after losing in Beijing, and came after she had led by a set and a break in Wuhan. Kartal next faces Jasmine Paolini.

content.headline: Martinez says United outburst came from anger as fallout continues
content.shortHeadline: Martinez explains United outburst as fallout continues
content.standfirst: Lisandro Martinez says he spoke out of frustration after Manchester United’s defeat by Atletico Madrid, but has not withdrawn his call for greater ambition. His comments leave Michael Carrick managing tension around recruitment and the club’s leadership.

image.caption: Jason Wilcox, Manchester United’s director of football.

sources.originalTitle: Martinez outburst came out of 'anger and frustration'
Wilcox the target again in another damaging Man Utd fallout

segments.body: Martinez said his criticism of Manchester United’s hierarchy followed from anger at the 2-0 defeat and a desire to see the club compete for major honours. He stopped short of apologising, reaffirmed his belief in his team-mates and manager Michael Carrick, and said players must also take responsibility.

segments.title: Questions over recruitment and the dressing room
segments.body: Martinez’s comments have reopened scrutiny of United’s recruitment and leadership, with Carrick needing to keep the squad focused after five games without a win. Martinez’s contract expires at the end of the season, and the club has an option to extend it by a year.

perspectives.body: BBC Sport reports that United sources do not expect director of football Jason Wilcox to lose his job, although the club accepts its summer recruitment strategy had shortcomings.

content.headline: Six Kings Slam postponed until December after deadly attacks in Riyadh
content.shortHeadline: Six Kings Slam postponed until December after Riyadh attacks
content.standfirst: The exhibition featuring Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev has been rescheduled for 27-30 December. Organisers cited logistical and organisational challenges; other Saudi sporting events have also been moved.

sources.originalTitle: Star-studded Saudi exhibition postponed after deadly attacks

segments.body: The Six Kings Slam, due to begin in Riyadh on 21 October, has been postponed until 27-30 December. Organisers cited logistical and organisational challenges after deadly attacks in Saudi Arabia, including a missile strike on Riyadh’s airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.

segments.title: Wider sporting disruption
segments.body: Three Saudi Pro League matches have also been rescheduled, while the Asian Tour says it is monitoring the situation ahead of its Saudi International in Riyadh in November. The source does not report a decision on that golf event.

content.headline: LIV accuses DP World Tour of interfering in its restructuring
content.shortHeadline: LIV accuses DP World Tour of interference
content.standfirst: LIV Golf says the DP World Tour’s plan to deny 2027 membership to players who intend to join LIV could interfere with its court-supervised restructuring. Its future format and player commitments remain unsettled.

sources.originalTitle: LIV accuses DP World Tour of player 'interference'

segments.body: At a court hearing, LIV’s lawyer said the tour was concerned that the DP World Tour’s membership stance could interfere with its restructuring and raise anti-competitive concerns. The DP World Tour declined to comment on that claim; its chief executive has said players need to make a choice about where they play.

segments.title: LIV’s future is not decided
segments.body: LIV’s lawyer told the court a decision on whether to continue as “LIV 2.0” or wind down was expected by the end of October. The organisation is seeking investment and enough player commitments; 19 player contracts, including those of Bryson DeChambeau and Dustin Johnson, were rejected during the hearing.

content.headline: Amy Cokayne returns as England’s unbeaten run faces Canada test
content.shortHeadline: Cokayne returns as England face Canada threat
content.standfirst: England’s 41-match unbeaten run is at risk against Rugby World Cup runners-up Canada in Toronto on Friday. Hooker Amy Cokayne returns after missing the previous Tests, following a 26-26 draw between the sides in Exeter.

image.caption: Amy Cokayne celebrates scoring for England against France.

sources.originalTitle: Cokayne back as England face Canada threat in Toronto

segments.body: Cokayne is back at hooker for England after last playing Test rugby in May. Bryony Field moves to the bench. Canada ended England’s near four-year winning streak with a 26-26 draw in Exeter last month, and coach Kevin Rouet has identified beating England as his team’s main aim for 2026.

segments.title: A different challenge away from home
segments.body: England coach John Mitchell said the Exeter Test had helped his side identify areas to improve, and described Toronto as a different environment and challenge. The teams are due to meet again in Ottawa on 23 October.

content.headline: Stevie Wonder gives Songs in the Key of Life a thrilling live life
content.shortHeadline: Stevie Wonder makes Songs in the Key of Life live
content.standfirst: On the opening night of a tour marking 50 years of the album, Wonder and a large ensemble play its songs with room to stretch and surprise. Their messages about inequality and empathy feel strikingly current.

image.caption: Stevie Wonder performing at Birmingham’s Utilita Arena.

sources.originalTitle: Stevie Wonder review – playing ​his greatest album in full, he knocks everyone sideways

segments.body: Stevie Wonder opened his Birmingham tour celebrating the 50th anniversary of Songs in the Key of Life by performing the album in full, with a large band and a string section. The show follows his earlier anniversary performances, but this is no attempt at a note-for-note replica: songs expand, new instrumental passages appear, and the band restarts Isn’t She Lovely at Wonder’s request.

The set’s quieter opening songs address a divided, unequal America; the Guardian review hears lyrics written in the mid-1970s speaking directly to 2026. The deep cuts are given space alongside the familiar celebrations of Sir Duke and I Wish, with the performance’s looseness and occasional imperfections adding to its force.

content.headline: A scrapbook and address book bring Brian Epstein’s 1967 into focus
content.shortHeadline: Brian Epstein’s address book reveals a life beyond the Beatles
content.standfirst: Gary Kemp and Simon Halfon turn Epstein’s contacts into an unconventional portrait of the Beatles’ manager in the year he died. The book traces his professional world and the loneliness and pressures that lay behind it.

image.caption: The Beatles with Brian Epstein at the premiere of A Hard Day’s Night in 1964.

sources.originalTitle: ‘He’s terrified, panicked, can’t sleep’: the tragic, lonely death of Beatles manager Brian Epstein

segments.body: A 1967 address book belonging to Beatles manager Brian Epstein inspired Spandau Ballet’s Gary Kemp and film-maker Simon Halfon to make a book about the people around him. Kemp bought it at auction for £10,710. Its 404 entries, many handwritten, prompted months of research into who Epstein knew and why.

segments.title: A portrait in fragments
segments.body: Rather than a conventional biography, 1967: The World of Brian Epstein and the Beatles assembles an account alphabetically from names, connections and fragments. The authors describe a manager trying to keep pace with the Beatles’ business while contending with addiction, isolation and the constraints of being gay when homosexuality was criminalised. The book’s picture of Epstein is necessarily reconstructed through his network and the authors’ research.

content.headline: Report says racial barriers in London live music cost up to £141m a year
content.shortHeadline: Report finds steep barriers for Black and south Asian music events
content.standfirst: A two-year study commissioned by the mayor’s office says Black and south Asian events face disproportionate cancellations, licensing restrictions and costs. Its authors call for clearer evidence and more transparent decisions.

image.caption: An image illustrating the report’s focus on unequal scrutiny of live music events.

sources.originalTitle: Barriers facing black and south Asian music events ‘cost London up to £141m a year’

segments.body: The Race Equality in Music Event Licensing report estimates that cancellations, displacement and events prevented from taking place cost London £127m to £141m a year. Its two-year investigation says genres including Afrobeats, drill and dancehall are routinely labelled high risk without credible evidence, while indie, pop and rock events face less scrutiny.

segments.title: Licensing and accountability
segments.body: Promoters told researchers that events can be cancelled on the basis of undisclosed or unverified police information, with little explanation and limited ways to challenge decisions. The report says these barriers can bring financial and reputational harm, and recommends evidence-based licensing, clearer reporting and stronger accountability. The Metropolitan Police said its contributions to licensing would be fair and evidence-based, while prioritising public safety.

content.headline: The Mary Wallopers turn grisly folk tales into a rowdy Edinburgh knees-up
content.shortHeadline: The Mary Wallopers make folk a rowdy, political knees-up
content.standfirst: The Irish group’s biggest tour yet pairs fast new songs with older traditions, irreverent politics and moments of unexpected stillness. At their Edinburgh opening night, the crowd moved from stamping jigs to listening closely.

image.caption: Charles Hendy of the Mary Wallopers performing onstage.

sources.originalTitle: The Mary Wallopers review – legs and pints go flying to the sound of rowdy folk ragers

segments.body: At the Edinburgh show opening their biggest tour, the Mary Wallopers turned Seán na Sagart—a song about an 18th-century hitman who targeted priests—into a crowd-surfing folk singalong. The six-piece’s new material also takes aim at capitalism, while the group’s humour and political edge give their unruly take on tradition a contemporary charge.

The band can also bring the room to a halt. A sparse version of Smuggling the Tin, led by uilleann pipes, and the slow march of Landlord’s Demise contrast with the high-speed songs. The review describes a set that makes room for both communal abandon and attention to the history and politics within the songs.

content.headline: Troye Sivan finds a looser, lonelier sound on She’s the Best
content.shortHeadline: Troye Sivan loosens his sound on She’s the Best
content.standfirst: Pitchfork hears the pop star moving beyond the dancefloor into more jagged, exposed songs. The shift yields some of his most affecting work, though the album’s experiments and references do not always cohere.

sources.originalTitle: She’s the Best

segments.body: On She’s the Best, Troye Sivan builds on the sample-led dance pop of Something to Give Each Other, but loosens its structures with bigger samples, harsher vocal effects and more dissonance. Pitchfork frames the album around the crash after stadium-scale performances: the rush of the crowd set against the solitude that follows.

segments.title: Where the feelings land
segments.body: The review finds the record strongest when Sivan leaves the dancefloor and sits with longing. “Le Boy,” “Embarrassingly” and “Love So Big It Hurts” give his emotional uncertainty room to unfold, while some spoken-word passages and the song “Party” feel underdeveloped. The result suggests a promising new direction without fully making it work across the album.

content.headline: Jess Williamson settles into country on searching album A Mile South of Heaven
content.shortHeadline: Jess Williamson finds her own country voice
content.standfirst: The Texas-born songwriter’s sixth album draws on outlaw country while reckoning with the pull of city and home. Pitchfork praises her newly assured singing and writing for holding those contradictions in view.

sources.originalTitle: A Mile South of Heaven

segments.body: A Mile South of Heaven pares back much of the indie-rock sheen of Jess Williamson’s earlier work. Produced by Shooter Jennings, the record places her supple vocals in warm country arrangements, while her Texas accent becomes part of the music’s character rather than a simple marker of authenticity.

The album moves between Los Angeles and Texas, and between the desire to leave and the ache of belonging. Pitchfork singles out Williamson’s detail-rich writing and a change in perspective on “Country Mile” as signs of an artist making music on her own terms, rather than trying to resolve the tensions in her life.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul reissue reveals an album still in motion
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul’s reissue shows there is no single definitive version
content.standfirst: A lavish new edition gathers alternate mixes, outtakes and recording notes around the Beatles’ pivotal 1965 album. Pitchfork argues that the material restores the record to human scale—and shows how its sound was shaped by both artistic choices and commercial pressures.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: The Rubber Soul Special Edition includes the UK and US album versions, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes, a new mix and an extensive recording history. The review follows the Beatles’ rushed November 1965 sessions, including the small arrangement choices that helped turn the album’s folk, pop and R&B influences into a coherent whole.

segments.title: Many versions, no final word
segments.body: The collection makes the album’s transformations audible: the US release changed the track listing, and the mono and stereo mixes give the arrangements different textures. Outtakes and studio exchanges complicate the idea that Rubber Soul was an inevitable masterpiece, presenting it instead as the work of musicians developing their ideas under deadline. The review concludes that listeners do not share one definitive version of the record.

content.headline: Joy Division’s live recordings reveal a thrilling side beneath the gloom
content.shortHeadline: Joy Division live: the thrill behind the band’s dark reputation
content.standfirst: A 16-disc collection gathers 19 performances recorded between 1979 and 1980. Pitchfork finds a band whose live energy and instrumental interplay complicate its austere image, while the recordings also trace how its sound developed.

sources.originalTitle: Eternal (Live)

segments.body: Eternal (Live) collects 19 recordings made from March 1979 to shortly before Ian Curtis’s death in May 1980. Without the icy studio production associated with Martin Hannett, the performances reveal more of the band’s rhythmic drive and the contrasting roles of Peter Hook’s melodic bass, Bernard Sumner’s guitar and Stephen Morris’s drums.

The performances range from the familiar force of “Transmission” to the band trying out different arrangements of “Love Will Tear Us Apart”. A 1980 Lyceum concert stands out for its run of later material, including “Isolation” and “Atrocity Exhibition”. The accompanying footage shows Curtis’s intense dancing alongside his control of the songs.

content.headline: NAZA review: anonymous Israeli intelligence accounts cast a chilling light on a
content.shortHeadline: NAZA examines anonymous Israeli accounts of the Gaza war
content.standfirst: In a documentary by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, Israeli intelligence personnel describe how targets are selected and civilian deaths calculated. The Guardian finds the testimony disturbing, while noting that anonymity limits its force.

image.caption: A night-time city view shown in the documentary NAZA.

sources.originalTitle: NAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deaths

segments.body: NAZA features Israeli intelligence personnel speaking anonymously, their faces and voices altered, about the war in Gaza. They allege that AI-assisted analysis of phone data helps identify targets and describe permitted error and expected civilian-death figures. These are claims made by the interviewees, not independently verified findings in the review.

segments.title: The limits of testimony
segments.body: The interviewees also discuss operations in northern Gaza and an intelligence unit they say is loyal to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The Guardian calls the film disquieting, but says its testimony is less forceful because no one appears under their own name or face. The review also rejects a speaker’s comparison with Nazism as ahistorical, while describing the film’s account of civilian harm as harrowing.

content.headline: La Bola Negra turns three stories of gay life in Spain into a sweeping epic
content.shortHeadline: La Bola Negra traces gay lives across a century of Spain
content.standfirst: Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s film links three gay men’s stories across 1932, 1937 and 2017. BBC Culture points to its formal ambition, performances and festival reception as reasons it is attracting awards attention.

sources.originalTitle: 'Immediately spellbinding': Four reasons why gay Spanish epic La Bola Negra could win the Oscar for best picture

segments.body: La Bola Negra follows a man serving in Franco’s army who loves a prisoner, a young man excluded from an elite club amid rumours about his sexuality, and a historian who receives an unexpected inheritance. The film connects their lives across a century of Spanish history, drawing inspiration from the work of Federico García Lorca.

segments.title: An awards-season contender
segments.body: The film won the People’s Choice Award at the Toronto Film Festival after receiving strong attention at Cannes, where it also won a directing prize. BBC Culture describes its blend of historical epic, romance and family drama, and notes its visual ambition, ensemble performances and budget of under $20m. Awards forecasts cited in the article place it among the leading best-picture contenders; the outcome remains uncertain.

content.headline: Why audiences may be tiring of Hollywood’s eat-the-rich satire
content.shortHeadline: Has Hollywood’s eat-the-rich satire run out of appetite?
content.standfirst: The Guardian argues that Digger’s commercial stumble may reflect more than divisive reviews: audiences could be weary of films that repeat familiar critiques of the wealthy. The subject remains relevant, but the satire may no longer feel fresh.

image.caption: Alejandro González Iñárritu and Tom Cruise at Digger’s Tokyo premiere.

sources.originalTitle: How we lost our appetite for eat-the-rich satire

segments.body: The Guardian places Digger’s reported box-office struggles within a broader cycle of eat-the-rich films, from Parasite’s influence to titles such as Saltburn and The Menu. It argues that the theme has not lost urgency, but that repeated cinematic reminders of inequality may leave viewers feeling they have heard the point before.

segments.title: A changing appetite
segments.body: The article suggests that doomscrolling delivers sharper, more immediate political satire than films that avoid specific headlines and risk preaching familiar ideas. It also notes the irony of Digger being the last film released by Warner Bros as an independent studio, ahead of a change in ownership. Its argument is an interpretation of audience fatigue, not proof of a single cause for the film’s performance.

content.headline: Winter of the Crow traps Lesley Manville in a surreal Warsaw thriller
content.shortHeadline: Lesley Manville is on edge in Winter of the Crow
content.standfirst: A British psychologist visiting Warsaw in 1981 becomes trapped as martial law takes hold. The Guardian praises the film’s uneasy atmosphere and surreal detail, while finding that its storytelling sometimes slows.

image.caption: Lesley Manville as Professor Andrews in Winter of the Crow.

sources.originalTitle: Winter of the Crow review – Lesley Manville magnificently on edge in intriguing cold war thriller

segments.body: Lesley Manville plays Professor Andrews, a British clinical psychologist invited to lecture in Warsaw in 1981. After losing her bag and passport, she is stranded in a tower-block district just as General Jaruzelski imposes martial law. The film turns her disorientation into a cold-war thriller with a Kafkaesque edge.

Directed by Kasia Adamik and adapted from a story by Olga Tokarczuk, the film mixes political menace with unsettling details, including a live carp kept in a bath before it is eaten. The Guardian finds the surreal touches part of the movie’s appeal, though it says the pace slackens and closer editing might have helped.

content.headline: Gary Waddell, the Australian actor who made small roles count, dies at 74
content.shortHeadline: Gary Waddell, Australian actor of unforgettable small roles, dies at
content.standfirst: Waddell spent decades in Australian film and television, often transforming brief appearances into vivid characters. A Guardian tribute recalls his breakthrough in Pure Shit and his performance in The King Is Dead!.

image.caption: Gary Waddell in The King Is Dead!.

sources.originalTitle: Gary Waddell dies aged 74: the brilliant Australian actor who turned small roles into great ones

segments.body: Gary Waddell, a fixture of Australian film and television for decades, has died aged 74. His early appearance in Bert Deling’s 1976 drug drama Pure Shit made an impression, and he went on to play supporting roles in productions including Chopper, Rake and The Survival of Kindness.

The Guardian tribute argues that Waddell brought unusual weight to small roles, recalling his performance as the volatile title character in The King Is Dead!. Waddell had said that substance abuse and self-doubt affected his early career; he later came to understand that his work on screen was a skill other actors studied.

content.headline: Kiri and Lou’s first feature is a gentle, tactile prehistoric adventure
content.shortHeadline: Kiri and Lou’s gentle stop-motion adventure wins over
content.standfirst: The CBeebies characters’ first feature-length outing tells how the unlikely friends met. The Guardian praises its concise storytelling, handmade animation and songs, making the film a strong family recommendation.

image.caption: Kiri and Lou, the prehistoric friends at the centre of the film.

sources.originalTitle: Kiri and Lou Go Raaa! review – delightful origin story for CBeebies’ prehistoric pals

segments.body: Kiri and Lou Go Raaa! introduces the origins of the friendship between a lively yellow dinosaur and a gentle purple creature. At an hour, the feature keeps its story accessible for young children, while returning viewers get a new chapter in the characters’ world.

The film combines voice performances from Olivia Tennet and Jemaine Clement with songs by Don McGlashan and tactile stop-motion. The Guardian says the physical quality of the models helps make the characters’ adventures feel tangible, rather than like figures floating in a digital world.

content.headline: Frank and Percy finds a tender, if sometimes sugary, romance in later life
content.shortHeadline: Ian McKellen and Roger Allam find late-life romance
content.standfirst: Ian McKellen and Roger Allam reprise their stage roles as two dog-walking men whose friendship turns to love. The Guardian finds warmth in their performances and Joanna Lumley’s supporting turn, despite some sentimentality.

image.caption: Ian McKellen as Percy and Roger Allam as Frank.

sources.originalTitle: Frank and Percy review – bromance becomes romance for dog walkers Ian McKellen and Roger Allam

segments.body: Roger Allam plays Frank, a widowed retired teacher; Ian McKellen is Percy, a sociologist separated from his partner. Their friendship grows on walks with their dogs, then takes an unexpected turn when Percy asks whether he can kiss Frank. The film adapts Ben Weatherill’s play, with both actors returning to their roles.

The Guardian describes the romance as a story about discovering desire and companionship later in life, supported by an all-star cast that includes Joanna Lumley as a woman living with early-onset dementia. It also notes the film’s sugary sentiment and broad supporting characters, but finds its easy-going warmth wins out.

content.headline: Wuthering Heights: The House of the Damned turns Brontë into dour horror
content.shortHeadline: Wuthering Heights gets a grisly but joyless horror makeover
content.standfirst: Becca Hirani’s adaptation adds supernatural visions and slasher violence to Emily Brontë’s novel. The Guardian finds the result too solemn to be fun and too garbled to make its horror convincing.

image.caption: Ross Townsend-Green as Mr Lockwood in Wuthering Heights: The House of the Damned.

sources.originalTitle: Wuthering Heights: The House of the Damned review – Brontë horror do-over is part Dracula, part Jeeves and Wooster

segments.body: In Wuthering Heights: The House of the Damned, Mr Lockwood’s visit to Heathcliff becomes a horror story of trapped guests, strange illnesses and the ghost of Catherine. The film follows some of the novel’s plot points but gives its characters far grislier fates and recasts Heathcliff as a killer.

The Guardian says the story is scattered through diary excerpts, testimony and flashbacks, leaving the manor’s history difficult to follow. It also finds that the film plays its gruesome material too straight, with performances that do not make Heathcliff’s turn to violence convincing. The review sees effort in the adaptation, but little reason for its reinvention.

content.headline: Time’s third series brings the crisis inside young offenders’ prisons into view
content.shortHeadline: Time turns its prison drama on young offenders
content.standfirst: David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran lead Jimmy McGovern’s latest prison drama, set in a young offenders’ institution. Two critics praise its performances and social urgency, while emphasising different aspects of its portrait of masculinity and confinement.

image.caption: David Tennant and Louis McCartney in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time review – David Tennant’s furious drama is as important as Adolescence
Time picks up where Adolescence left off

segments.body: The third series of Time is set in a young offenders’ institution where boys can be locked in their cells for 23 hours a day under a system intended to keep certain prisoners apart. David Tennant plays a worn-down but compassionate officer; Siobhan Finneran returns as a chaplain whose faith has faltered. The Guardian review says the drama shows how isolation and institutional pressure can intensify violence.

perspectives.body: The i Paper places the series within a wider run of dramas about masculinity, arguing that prison conditions can entrench the aggression they are meant to contain. It highlights the lack of education and other support for young prisoners as part of the problem.

segments.body: Both reviews praise the young cast and the drama’s refusal to excuse serious violence. The Guardian stresses the series’ emotional power and its insistence that connection can offer some hope; the i Paper focuses on how the boys and their guards struggle to express vulnerability except through force. The reviews see no easy remedy in the story.

content.headline: Girls will return to HBO for a five-episode reunion in 2027
content.shortHeadline: Girls returns with its original cast for five episodes
content.standfirst: Lena Dunham, Allison Williams, Zosia Mamet, Jemima Kirke and Andrew Rannells will reunite for a limited run a decade after the series finale. Plot and title details have not yet been announced.

image.caption: The cast of Girls.

sources.originalTitle: Lena Dunham’s Girls returning for limited run at HBO

segments.body: HBO has ordered five new episodes of Girls, with creator and star Lena Dunham returning alongside Allison Williams, Zosia Mamet, Jemima Kirke and Andrew Rannells. Production is planned for next year, with the series set to return in 2027, ten years after its finale.

Dunham said the team had wanted a specific story before revisiting the characters and that the idea came into focus around her fortieth birthday. Further details—including the plot and whether the revival will keep the Girls title—are still unknown. The original six-season series received 19 Emmy nominations and two wins.

content.headline: VisionQuest’s inventive ideas are buried under Marvel lore and exposition
content.shortHeadline: VisionQuest is clever but lost in its own Marvel machinery
content.standfirst: The WandaVision spin-off gives Paul Bettany’s android a story about identity, but the Guardian finds its ambition crowded out by plot, lore and lengthy dialogue. Its visual experimentation does not fully overcome the franchise’s familiar excesses.

image.caption: James Spader as Ultron and Paul Bettany as The Vision in VisionQuest.

sources.originalTitle: VisionQuest review – Marvel’s latest TV show feels like it could have been made by a computer

segments.body: VisionQuest follows The Vision as he tries to understand his identity, with his memories restored but his feelings absent. The series brings him into contact with a group of AI personalities, including Ultron, while a teenager who may be connected to his family becomes part of a flight from a bounty hunter.

segments.title: A difficult balance
segments.body: The Guardian credits the series with visual invention and a willingness to shift between genres, but says its many plot strands and references make it hard to follow without substantial Marvel homework. The AI dialogue is often laboured, and the action and exposition drown out the show’s questions about humanity and selfhood.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors makes fame and likeability part of the game
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors turns likeability into a liability
content.standfirst: Maya Jama is thriving as a Traitor while James Acaster and Hannah Fry hesitate over the role. Three i Paper columns examine the game’s celebrity-specific pressures, from strategic suspicion to the discomfort of turning on fellow players.

image.caption: Maya Jama, one of the Traitors in the celebrity edition.

sources.originalTitle: Maya Jama has one big problem
Hannah Fry is too clever for her own good
The Celebrity Traitors is starting to get very uncomfortable

segments.body: The i Paper’s coverage of The Celebrity Traitors finds Maya Jama taking charge after Richard E Grant’s departure, while James Acaster and Hannah Fry are uneasy about betraying players they care about. Jama has to decide whether to help them adapt or protect her own position by turning against them.

segments.title: A game of reputations
segments.body: The columns argue that celebrity contestants face a particular risk: the skills needed to accuse, manipulate and form alliances can conflict with public personas built on being liked. Hannah Fry’s intelligence may help her read the game, but it also makes her a conspicuous target; other writers focus on Jama’s strategic control and the emotional discomfort of watching innocent players get banished.

perspectives.body: The i Paper argues that the game’s unpleasantness is revealing: celebrity players must risk looking like bullies, while viewers can see how assumptions about trust and belonging shape who gets accused.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after the Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after Disney+ exit
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its co-production partnership with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking new funding for the series. Fans and industry voices disagree on what went wrong, while no new Doctor or return date has been confirmed.

image.caption: Illustrations of several actors who have played the Doctor.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: After the 2025 series starring Ncuti Gatwa, Doctor Who has no confirmed next episode. The BBC has ended its partnership with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and put future production out to competitive tender. No company has yet stepped forward, and the BBC has declined to discuss the decision in detail.

The i Paper traces the show’s long history of pauses, revivals and changing leads, and considers possible causes of the latest setback, from scripts and leadership to the end of the streaming partnership. Lifelong fan Frank Skinner argues that the programme did not need a major Disney investment simply to tell a good story. The future remains unresolved, but contributors expect the series to return eventually.

content.headline: Sarah Solemani’s The Party turns a class-system story into a family drama
content.shortHeadline: Sarah Solemani brings class and ambition to The Party
content.standfirst: The actor, writer and showrunner discusses adapting Elizabeth Day’s novel for ITV, her experience of bereavement and how #MeToo changed Hollywood sets. The new drama centres on a birthday party where a working-class journalist meets his old friend, a Tory politician.

image.caption: Sarah Solemani, actor, writer and showrunner of The Party.

sources.originalTitle: Sarah Solemani: ‘I performed at my mum’s hospice bed two weeks before she died’

segments.body: The Party, adapted from Elizabeth Day’s novel, follows working-class journalist Martin and politician Ben, former friends with a dark secret, at Ben’s fortieth birthday. Sarah Solemani plays Martin’s pregnant wife, Lucy, and also wrote and showran the series. She says the class system remains part of British life, including for people who have moved abroad.

segments.title: A career shaped by loss and change
segments.body: Solemani recalls performing monologues at her mother’s hospice bed at 16, two weeks before her mother died, and receiving an acceptance letter from the National Youth Theatre the following day. She also says #MeToo dismantled an old Hollywood system and describes changes on set, including the introduction of intimacy supervisors.

content.headline: Ellie Taylor on taking Strictly’s It Takes Two into a new era
content.shortHeadline: Ellie Taylor brings a comic touch to It Takes Two
content.standfirst: The comedian and former Strictly contestant has taken over the BBC spin-off, aiming to make it part of the wider conversation around the main show. She discusses viewer feedback, social anxiety and why she is content with the role.

image.caption: Ellie Taylor, the new host of It Takes Two.

sources.originalTitle: Ellie Taylor on the Strictly backlash: ‘People don’t like change’

segments.body: Ellie Taylor has become the new host of Strictly Come Dancing: It Takes Two. A former contestant, she says she wants the spin-off to lean into the show’s humour and connect with its wider audience. After viewers questioned a panel without professional dancers, she introduced a panel of pros the next day.

Taylor says presenting the spin-off is a “dream gig” and that her stand-up experience helps her move between scripted material and improvisation. She also discusses social anxiety and says she is happy with the job, despite having auditioned for the main Saturday-night presenting role.

content.headline: Ocarina of Time remake asks how much a classic should change
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time returns with a new look and new controls
content.standfirst: A hands-on preview of Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake finds a more responsive Link, an orchestrated soundtrack and a striking visual overhaul. The familiar puzzles remain, but the new character design may divide fans.

image.caption: Link in Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era

segments.body: Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake gives Link a manual jump, a sprint, a freely moving camera and updated aiming, alongside a newly orchestrated soundtrack. The Guardian’s preview finds the controls make the 1998 adventure feel different under the thumbs, even when the improvements are now common in other games.

segments.title: A classic in a new frame
segments.body: The preview describes the remake as a polished return to Hyrule’s traditional dungeons and puzzles, while noting that its 4K scenery cannot recreate the original’s shock of discovery. Link’s glossy, doll-like appearance has prompted criticism, though the article considers whether it might draw on Japanese puppetry rather than simply pursuing visual realism.

content.headline: Could independent arcades bring a more social kind of gaming back?
content.shortHeadline: A new generation of arcades could make gaming social again
content.standfirst: After years of sprawling games designed to hold players’ time, a smaller arcade-inspired movement is taking shape. The Guardian’s games writer sees potential in curated venues that bring local communities back into gaming.

image.caption: A games arcade finding a new audience.

sources.originalTitle: Ready player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirth

segments.body: The Guardian argues that players and developers are showing renewed interest in shorter, more focused games, in contrast with “forever games” built around constant updates. It points to new titles influenced by arcade design and to a growing number of gaming bars and independent venues.

segments.title: More than coin-operated nostalgia
segments.body: Games journalist Will Freeman says a handful of venues are moving beyond the familiar bar-and-retro-cabinet model. The article highlights London’s forthcoming NQ Japan and Pixel Bunker in Milton Keynes as examples of places that could curate games and foster enthusiast communities. Whether a broader network will develop remains an open question.

content.headline: What GTA 6’s £350 collector’s box says about gaming’s rising costs
content.shortHeadline: GTA 6’s £350 collector’s box signals a luxury gaming market
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s merchandise set costs £350 and does not include the game. The Guardian argues that such premium extras reflect a widening divide between low-cost mobile play and console or PC gaming, which is increasingly expensive to access.

image.caption: The Grand Theft Auto VI collector’s merchandise box.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s £350 Grand Theft Auto VI collector’s box includes merchandise but no game or download code. Add the reported £70 game price and the total is £420. The Guardian writer says the box is not for them to judge, but notes that this is unusually expensive compared with many earlier special editions.

segments.title: Who can afford to play?
segments.body: The article links the price to a wider rise in console, game and merchandise costs. Citing Newzoo, it says about 80% of players play free or at low cost on mobile, while a smaller group accounts for a disproportionate share of spending in the high-end market. The concern is that games as detailed, persistent worlds may become a luxury hobby.

content.headline: Silver Pines turns noir and survival horror into a stylish detective mystery
content.shortHeadline: Silver Pines is a moody detective mystery worth exploring
content.standfirst: The Guardian recommends a 2D adventure about a private investigator searching for a missing musician in a deserted town. Its puzzles and combat are familiar, but the detailed visual design and slow-burn atmosphere give it a strong identity.

image.caption: A scene from the neo-noir game Silver Pines.

sources.originalTitle: Silver Pines review – a stylish, neo-noir detective drama

segments.body: Silver Pines casts players as private eye Red Walker, searching for a missing singer-songwriter in a town emptied ahead of a storm. Payphones, clues and locked locations lead deeper into a mystery, while limited ammunition and fragile weapons bring survival-horror tension to the exploration.

segments.title: A world of its own
segments.body: The Guardian praises the game’s rotoscoped character animation, carefully lit rooms and references to noir and 1980s and 1990s screen culture, including Twin Peaks and Blue Velvet. Its puzzles can be obscure and combat deliberately awkward, but lowering the difficulty lets players focus on the story and atmosphere.

content.headline: Playing Call of Duty with his son brings a father back to their first game
content.shortHeadline: A father and son return to the game that began it all
content.standfirst: A father revisits Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 with his now 22-year-old son, nearly two decades after their first co-op sessions. What begins as a test of old missions becomes a reflection on gaming, family and time together.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game father and son played together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The Guardian writer and his 22-year-old son return to the Special Ops missions they first played together when the son was five. This time, the father’s cautious scouting and his son’s rush into combat slowly give way to teamwork, and they finally beat missions that defeated them years ago.

The essay is less about mastering a shooter than recovering the pleasure of playing together. With their time living in the same flat due to end in a few months, the writer’s son says he expects to remember these sessions as some of their best times. The father admits the games have brought him to tears.

content.headline: GTA 6’s virtual romance debate reflects real relationship anxieties
content.shortHeadline: Is a GTA 6 romance cheating—or a sign of a deeper worry?
content.standfirst: Online arguments say maintaining a relationship between the game’s protagonists counts as infidelity. The i Paper rejects that as a universal rule, but argues that fears about virtual romance can point to loneliness and unmet needs in real relationships.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the couple at the centre of GTA 6’s romance system.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: Grand Theft Auto VI asks players to strengthen the bond between Lucia and Jason through gestures such as dates, messages and time together. Some social-media users say that participating in the romance is a form of cheating. The article notes that in-game romance is not new, and that players engage with both characters’ relationships.

segments.title: Boundaries beyond the game
segments.body: The i Paper argues that dismissing all concerns as jealousy misses the insecurity some people may feel when a partner invests attention in a fictional relationship. Its writer does not consider game romances cheating, while stressing that boundaries differ. The debate, the article suggests, points to loneliness and dissatisfaction that a game cannot resolve.

content.headline: The White House arcade uses familiar games to push anti-migrant propaganda
content.shortHeadline: The White House turns arcade games into anti-migrant propaganda
content.standfirst: The Guardian examines a set of games on the US government’s website that rework familiar titles into political messaging. Its writer calls some of them dehumanising and argues that the move shows how gaming aesthetics can be weaponised.

image.caption: A screenshot from Build the Wall, one of the White House arcade games.

sources.originalTitle: The Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcade

segments.body: The White House website’s arcade includes games that borrow from familiar formats. Build the Wall recasts Tetris as a border-fortification challenge, while Rio Run has players collect pixelated migrants. The Guardian describes the games as part of a wider effort by the Trump administration to use video-game imagery in its messaging.

segments.title: Politics in play
segments.body: The article argues that the games are more effective as provocation than persuasion, but says their release marks a step from using gaming references in social-media posts to turning games themselves into political content. Games scholar George Osborn links the approach to the political right’s history in online game communities. The writer’s suggestion that the games may have been made with AI is speculation, not a confirmed production detail.

content.headline: A sharper ear may help language learners master unfamiliar sounds
content.shortHeadline: A sharper ear may help learners master new language sounds
content.standfirst: A study of Japanese learners of English links better pitch, length and tone discrimination with faster, more accurate pronunciation. The researchers say language teaching could give listening skills more attention.

image.caption: A language learner listens to unfamiliar speech sounds.

sources.originalTitle: Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggests

segments.body: Researchers compared 67 Japanese learners of English, testing their ability to detect small changes in pitch, length and tone and using brain scans as participants distinguished English vowels absent from Japanese. Those with higher auditory precision learned unfamiliar pronunciation faster and more accurately.

segments.title: What the findings suggest
segments.body: Learners with greater sound sensitivity relied less on brain activity associated with processing their native language when hearing foreign sounds. Lead author Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren said the results challenge the idea that some populations are inherently poor at languages, and suggest teaching should develop learners’ ears as well as vocabulary and grammar.

perspectives.body: Lancaster University’s Padraic Monaghan said the study underlines the importance of listening and exposure, while noting that learners vary in their sensitivity to new sounds, particularly in the early stages.

content.headline: Could computer-made birdsong help restore songs lost as populations decline?
content.shortHeadline: Could computer-made birdsong help restore lost songs?
